Kant didn't extend this principle to animals, but philosophers such as Tom Regan argued that every subject-of-a-life has value of their own and can't be treated as a mere resource. That is what happens in animal farming, where the animal's whole life is organized around what they produce. In the political sense, people also speak of instrumentalizing a cause, for example when animal protection is used only to attack the practices of minority groups, while those of the majority are left out. See Instrumental value, Intrinsic value, Objectification and Subjects-of-a-life.

def: A situation in which objective facts are less influential in shaping public opinion than appeals to emotion and personal belief.
com: The term was chosen as word of the year for 2016 by Oxford Dictionaries, the year of the Brexit referendum and the US presidential election. It isn't the same as fake news: fake news is the content, and post-truth is the climate in which it circulates and convinces, because it confirms what people already want to believe. In the debate about animals, it appears on both sides: in advertisements of happy cows that don't show the reality of farms, in nutrition myths that spread on social media, and also in exaggerations by animal advocates. The antidote is the same for everyone: verifiable sources, attention to what scientific bodies say, including where they disagree, and willingness to admit uncertainty. See Truth, Evidence and Cognitive dissonance.

def: The set of companies and activities that breed, slaughter, process and sell animals as meat, from genetics and feed to meatpacking plants, distribution and advertising.
com: It is one of the largest industries in the world: according to FAO data, more than 80 billion land animals are slaughtered each year for consumption, not counting fish, which are measured in tonnes. The sector is concentrated in a few companies, and one of them, Brazil's JBS, is the largest meat processor in the world; Brazil is also the largest exporter of beef and chicken. To protect its prices and image, the industry relies on lobbying, subsidies and advertising with happy animals, fights in court over the use of names like "burger" for plant-based products and, in the United States, backed laws that punish those who secretly film farms, several of which courts have struck down. The costs it doesn't pay fall on others: cattle ranching is the main driver of deforestation in the Amazon, and meatpacking workers face high rates of injury and psychological distress. Criticizing the industry isn't accusing each worker or small producer, who often have few alternatives. See Livestock industry, Industrial livestock farming, Lobby, Subsidies and Externality.

def: What leaves a being worse off than they would otherwise be; in the moral sense, a setback to someone's interests.
com: There are two ways of causing harm: bringing about something bad, such as pain, fear or disease, which is intrinsic harm, or taking away something good, such as freedom, companionship or the rest of one's life, which is extrinsic harm, or harm by deprivation. In the moral sense, only those who have interests, that is, sentient beings, can be harmed: a car can be damaged, but there is no one for whom that is bad. In law, the word has its own uses, as in material and moral damages. See Intrinsic harm, Extrinsic harm, Harm of death, Maleficence and Benefit.

def: Harm that is bad in itself for the one who suffers it, regardless of its consequences, such as pain, fear, distress and boredom.
com: It is the easiest kind of harm to recognize, because it is felt: an animal mutilated without anaesthesia or confined in a space where they can barely move suffers an intrinsic harm. Many animal welfare reforms try to reduce only this kind of harm, and leave aside extrinsic harm, such as death. See Harm, Extrinsic harm and Suffering.

def: Harm that is not bad in itself, but because of what it prevents or causes; the main case is deprivation, when something good someone would have had is taken away.
com: An extrinsic harm can happen without any pain: a quick death takes away all the good experiences to come, and comfortable confinement takes away freedom, exploration of the environment and companionship. That's why the question "what if the animal doesn't suffer?" doesn't settle the debate: even without intrinsic harm, there can be serious extrinsic harm. Also called harm by deprivation. See Harm, Intrinsic harm and Harm of death.

def: What leaves a being better off than they would otherwise be, either by giving them something good, such as pleasure, health or companionship, or by preventing something bad.
com: In bioethics, the principle of beneficence asks us to act for the good of others, and it is one of the four principles proposed by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress in 1979, alongside respect for autonomy, non-maleficence and justice. In the debate about animals, the question is often whether the benefits of a use outweigh the harms it causes. Often the benefit to humans is small, such as taste or convenience, and the harm to animals is enormous, such as a life of confinement and death. See Harm, Maleficence and Interest.

def: The evil or harm done to someone; the opposite of benefit.
com: In bioethics, the principle of non-maleficence, "first, do no harm", is one of the oldest in medical ethics. Applied consistently, it asks us not to cause unnecessary harm to any being who can suffer it, which includes animals. See Harm, Benefit and Bioethics.

def: Liberty as the absence of interference: to be free is not to be prevented or coerced by others.
com: The distinction between negative and positive liberty became well known through the philosopher Isaiah Berlin, in the 1958 essay *Two Concepts of Liberty*. For animals, negative liberty is the most obvious: not being locked in cages, crates or tanks, not being tied up, not being forced to work or perform. But it isn't enough: an animal released in a place where they can't survive suffers no interference and can still suffer greatly. See Freedom, Positive liberty and Five Freedoms.

def: Liberty as the capacity to act: to be free is to have real conditions to make choices and run one's own life.
com: For Isaiah Berlin, positive liberty was above all self-determination, being one's own master; today the term also covers having the means to act, such as health, resources and a suitable environment. For animals, it helps explain why opening the cages isn't enough: rescued animals need care and a place where they can live well, and wild animals free from human interference can still go hungry, fall ill and suffer. It is one of the reasons part of the movement argues for helping animals in the wild when this is possible without causing more harm. See Freedom, Negative liberty and Wild animal suffering.

def: Influencing someone's beliefs or choices by means that bypass or exploit their capacity to evaluate, such as deceiving, hiding information, exploiting biases and emotions or applying pressure, instead of offering good reasons.
com: The difference from persuasion lies in the means, not the goal: those who persuade present reasons and evidence the other person can examine and reject; those who manipulate count on them not noticing what is happening. Appealing to emotions isn't, in itself, manipulation: showing how animals live on a factory farm is true and relevant, and the emotion it arouses is part of understanding the problem. It becomes manipulation when the image is fake or out of context, when the numbers are exaggerated, or when guilt and shame are used to stop the person from thinking. The line isn't always sharp, and philosophers debate how to draw it. Both sides of the debate can manipulate: the industry, with euphemisms and adverts of happy animals, and animal advocates, with inflated statistics. For a cause that asks for consistency, persuading honestly is also a matter of respect. See Mass manipulation, Euphemism, Post-truth and Autonomy.

def: Manipulation aimed at large audiences, through the press, advertising, political propaganda, social media and other means of communication.
com: One of the pioneers of public relations, Edward Bernays, argued in his book *Propaganda* (1928) that public opinion could be deliberately shaped, and by his own account helped popularize the bacon-and-eggs breakfast in the United States, in a campaign for a bacon producer backed by doctors' opinions. Twentieth-century totalitarian regimes used propaganda on a large scale, and today social media allow messages tailored to each profile, as the Cambridge Analytica case showed in 2018. In food, industry campaigns helped associate meat and milk with strength, health and tradition, while showing little of how animals live and die. Two cautions apply: not all mass communication is manipulation, and saying that those who disagree "have been manipulated" doesn't answer their arguments; it can also be a way of dodging the debate. See Manipulation, Post-truth, Meat industry and Carnism.

def: Absorbing an opponent, a movement or an idea by offering positions, advantages, recognition or partnerships, so that it stops challenging and starts serving the interests of whoever co-opted it.
com: In the animal cause, the concern takes several forms: welfare labels and partnerships that make exploitation more acceptable without reducing it, words like "humane" and "sustainable" used in industry marketing, and large meat companies buying or launching plant-based brands. Not all of this is co-optation: talking to companies, supporting reforms and seeing meatpackers sell plant-based products can help animals, and the movement debates when it helps and when it hinders. The useful test is to ask whether the partnership brings the end of exploitation closer or pushes it away, and whether those invited to the table can still say no. See Political pawns, Lobby, Welfarism and Manipulation.

def: People used for others' ends, without realizing it or without control over it, for example as support in mobilizations, as votes or as a base for pressure.
com: In English the idea appears in several forms: "pawns", "useful idiots", a harsher term that implies naive supporters, and "astroturfing", the practice of faking grassroots support, for example when an industry funds groups that appear to be spontaneous citizens' movements. Brazilian Portuguese says "massa de manobra". All of these are pejorative, and calling someone a pawn is often a way of dismissing them without answering what they say. Still, the phenomenon exists: economic sectors can mobilize small farmers and workers against rules whose costs and benefits fall unequally, and movements on any side can use supporters without explaining their goals. In the debate about animals, the same caution as with manipulation applies: discuss the arguments of those who mobilize, rather than assuming they disagree only because they were used. See Co-optation, Mass manipulation and Manipulation.

def: An animal, such as a donkey, mule, horse or ox, used to carry loads or pull carts; figuratively, a person made to do the heavy work without recognition.
com: Donkeys and mules still carry loads and pull carts in many regions, often with wounds, excessive weight and little water and rest. In recent years they have also been slaughtered in large numbers for the trade in skins used in ejiao, a traditional Chinese medicine product, which has led several countries to restrict this trade. English has a whole family of figurative expressions from working animals: "workhorse", "pack mule", "work like a dog", "treated like a beast of burden". Brazilian Portuguese says "burro de carga". They all show how normalized animal exploitation is: saying a person is "treated like a beast of burden" denounces an abuse against them, but assumes the same treatment is normal for the animal. See Animal traction, Speciesist term and Objectification.

def: A word or expression that treats animals as things, uses animal names as insults or makes exploitation seem normal.
com: In English there are several kinds: calling animals "it", "stock" or "head"; using "pig", "cow", "chicken", "rat", "snake" or "dumb animal" as insults, which assumes those animals are inferior; calling people in experiments "guinea pigs"; and idioms that normalize violence, such as "kill two birds with one stone", "beat a dead horse", "there's more than one way to skin a cat" or "like lambs to the slaughter". Simple alternatives exist, such as "solve two problems at once", "go over old ground" or "there's more than one way to do it". In 2018, PETA proposed playful swaps such as "feed two birds with one scone", and was widely mocked, which shows how easily the subject can backfire. Language reflects and reinforces attitudes, and noticing these terms helps us see how common speciesism is. But changing words doesn't change practices by itself, and constantly correcting other people's speech can push away those who are just starting to think about the subject. See Euphemism, Absent referent, Objectification, Beast of burden and Guinea pig.

def: The domestic guinea pig (Cavia porcellus), a small rodent domesticated in the Andes thousands of years ago; by extension, any animal used in experiments and, figuratively, any person subjected to a test.
com: The guinea pig was one of the first laboratory animals: in the late 18th century, Lavoisier and Laplace used one to measure the heat produced by the body, and in the early 20th century it was central to research on scurvy, because, like humans, it can't make its own vitamin C. Today mice and rats are used far more, but the name stuck as a synonym for an experimental animal. Guinea pigs are also kept as companion animals and, in the Andes, raised as food. The figurative sense, as in "being used as a guinea pig", follows the same pattern as other speciesist terms: using someone in tests without their consent is seen as abuse when it is a person, but as normal when it is the animal who gave the expression its name. In Portuguese the word is "cobaia". See Animal experimentation, Animal model, 3Rs and Speciesist term.

def: A member of the species Homo sapiens, a primate that emerged in Africa about 300,000 years ago and is the only living species of the genus Homo; also called a human.
com: Biologically, a human being is an animal, and the opposition "humans and animals" is a convention of language. The word "humane" took on a moral sense of kindness and compassion, and "inhumane" became a synonym for cruel, as if mistreatment were typical of other animals. The ethical question isn't whether humans are special, because they have unique abilities, but whether those abilities justify ignoring the interests of those who lack them. The same criteria that protect all humans, including babies and people with profound cognitive disabilities, such as the capacity to feel, also apply to many other animals. Defending animals doesn't diminish human rights; it extends the same logic. See Animal, Nonhuman animal, Anthropocentrism and Speciesism.

def: An approach to raising and teaching, children and also animals, based on respect, encouragement and reinforcing the desired behaviour, rather than punishment, fear and pain.
com: With children, the name often refers to positive discipline, proposed by the psychologist Jane Nelsen in the 1980s based on the ideas of Alfred Adler, which aims to be firm and kind at the same time; it is also used for Martin Seligman's positive education, which brings well-being into schools. Research links physical punishment to worse outcomes for children, and in Brazil the 2014 Menino Bernardo Law bans physical punishment and cruel treatment in child rearing. With animals, the equivalent idea is positive reinforcement training, which rewards the desired behaviour; studies find more signs of stress in dogs trained with aversive methods, such as shock collars and leash jerks. See Animal training and Humane education.

def: Applying different criteria to similar cases, as suits whoever is judging. The Portuguese expression is "dois pesos e duas medidas" (two weights and two measures).
com: It is a form of inconsistency and the opposite of moral universality. In the treatment of animals, it is very common: the same act is a crime against a dog and routine against a pig, other peoples' hunting is barbaric and ours is tradition, the suffering of a cute animal moves us and that of a fish goes unnoticed. Pointing out a double standard doesn't show which of the two treatments is right, but it shows that at least one of them has to change. And the demand applies to animal advocates too: the same yardstick should be applied to one's own choices. See Moral consistency, Moral universality, Speciesism and Cultural relativism.

def: Giving special weight to the interests of some, such as family, friends, compatriots or one's own companion animals, because of the relationship we have with them.
com: Some partiality is accepted by almost everyone: caring for one's own children before strangers' children doesn't seem wrong. Philosophers such as Bernard Williams criticized theories that demand total impartiality, and the ethics of care values close relationships. Brian Barry, in *Justice as Impartiality* (1995), distinguished two levels: first-order partiality, in everyday choices, can be legitimate, but second-order rules and public policies must be impartial, because the state cannot hand out protection according to the affections of those who govern. The limit lies elsewhere: partiality can justify helping those close to us more, but not harming those far away. Loving one's own dog is legitimate partiality; paying for pigs to suffer isn't a way of caring for anyone. Partiality also becomes injustice when the criterion is arbitrary, such as skin colour or species, rather than a real relationship. See Impartiality, Ethics of care, Mixed community, Double standard and Speciesism.

def: In activism, quick, cheap and surprising actions carried out by small groups to draw attention where and when it isn't expected, such as projections on buildings, banners, street interventions and flash demonstrations.
com: The term comes from irregular warfare: "guerrilla" means "little war" in Spanish and became popular during the resistance to Napoleon's occupation of Spain in the early 19th century, with small, mobile groups that avoided direct confrontation with a larger army. In activism, the idea is to make up for a lack of resources with creativity and surprise. There is an important difference between legal, peaceful actions and actions that damage property or intimidate people. And the effect isn't always what was intended: a 2020 study by Matthew Feinberg, Robb Willer and Chloe Kovacheff found that protest tactics seen as extreme tend to reduce public support for the cause, even when they draw more attention. See Guerrilla marketing, Direct action, Protest and Vigil.

def: An unconventional, low-cost form of promotion that uses creativity, surprise and public spaces to draw attention, instead of paid advertising.
com: The term was popularized by Jay Conrad Levinson in his book *Guerrilla Marketing* (1984), written for small businesses. Social movements adopted the same logic. In the animal cause, a well-known example is the Cube of Truth, by the group Anonymous for the Voiceless, founded in Australia in 2016: masked activists, standing in a cube formation, hold screens showing footage from farms and slaughterhouses while others talk to passers-by who stop. Projections, stickers, art interventions and online actions also fall into this category. Creativity doesn't excuse dishonesty: footage must be genuine and in context, and the effect of each action should be evaluated, not assumed. See Guerrilla tactics, Manipulation, Street activism and Vegan witness (bearing witness).

def: In animal advocacy, a peaceful gathering outside slaughterhouses, farms or animal markets to bear witness to the animals' suffering, record it and make it visible.
com: The format became known through Toronto Pig Save, founded in Canada in 2010 by Anita Krajnc, which grew into the Animal Save Movement, now with groups in many countries. At vigils, activists look at the animals arriving in trucks, photograph and film them, and sometimes give them water when drivers stop. In 2015, Krajnc was charged for giving water to pigs in a truck, and she was acquitted in 2017. Vigils usually follow safety and non-violence rules, but they carry risks: in 2020, the activist Regan Russell was killed by a truck transporting pigs during a vigil in Ontario. For many participants, a vigil is also an act of mourning and a refusal to look away. See Vegan witness (bearing witness), Protest and Guerrilla tactics.

def: A lifestyle that seeks to own and consume less, keeping what is useful or meaningful and letting go of excess.
com: The name comes from the minimalist art of the 1960s, and the lifestyle became popular in the 2010s, through books, blogs and documentaries such as those by the duo The Minimalists. It has points in common with veganism: buying less, choosing second-hand and repairing instead of replacing reduce environmental impact, and many minimalists question the idea that consuming more brings happiness. But the two aren't the same. Minimalism asks how much is consumed; veganism asks what is consumed and who pays for it. A minimalist can own few things and still eat meat or wear leather, and a vegan can consume a lot. Some also criticize minimalism when it becomes just an aesthetic, with expensive products sold as simplicity. See Conscious consumption, Consumption and Veganism.

def: A way of studying aimed at memorizing and reproducing information, without seeking to understand its meaning or connect the ideas.
com: The distinction between surface and deep learning comes from the Swedish researchers Ference Marton and Roger Säljö in the 1970s. Memorizing has its place: knowing the short answer to an objection by heart helps in a quick conversation. The problem is stopping there. Someone who memorized an answer often gets stuck when the objection comes in another form, or when the other person makes the next reply. See Deep learning, Declarative (or explicit) knowledge and Critical thinking.

def: A way of studying aimed at understanding the meaning, the reasons and the links between ideas, and applying them to new situations.
com: In argumentation, it is the difference between memorizing that an argument is wrong and understanding why it fails, which premise is false or which principle would lead to conclusions the person themselves rejects. That understanding makes it possible to recognize the same error in new forms. That's why the guide offers layers: the short answer to use now and the full answer, with the best counter-reply, for those who want to understand. Not to be confused with deep learning in artificial intelligence, a machine learning technique; in education the term is also called a deep approach to learning. See Surface learning, Critical thinking and Procedural knowledge.

def: A person who knows a little about many fields and can connect what they learn in each.
com: Animal ethics cuts across many fields, such as philosophy, nutrition, ecology, law, economics and psychology, and a generalist sees connections a specialist may miss. The political scientist Philip Tetlock, studying expert predictions, found that those he called "foxes", who know many things and combine several perspectives, tended to do better than the "hedgehogs", attached to one big idea. The generalist's risk is superficiality: on technical questions, such as nutrition or fish welfare, it pays to consult those who study the subject in depth. See Specialist and Deep learning.

def: A person with in-depth, recognized knowledge in a field, acquired through training, research or long experience.
com: Trusting specialists is reasonable, because no one can check everything alone. But there are cautions: authority holds within each person's field, and a doctor isn't an expert in ethics nor a philosopher in nutrition; the consensus of many specialists weighs more than the opinion of one; and specialists also have biases and conflicts of interest, as when research is funded by those who profit from the result. Citing a specialist outside their field, or a lone one against the consensus, is what is called an appeal to authority. See Generalist, Evidence and Ethicist.

def: Someone who examines and evaluates something, pointing out strengths and flaws; as the adjective "critical", what involves that examination, as in critical thinking, or what is decisive, as in a critical moment.
com: Being critical isn't being contrarian: good criticism acknowledges what is right before pointing out what is wrong, which is why the guide shows, for each argument, what it gets right. Critics of veganism aren't enemies to defeat, and many of their objections raise real points. Likewise, animal advocates need to accept criticism, including from within the movement, to correct mistakes and improve their arguments. See Critical thinking, Anti-vegan and Skepticism.

def: Knowledge of facts and ideas that can be stated, written down and taught in words; "knowing that", such as knowing that fish have nociceptors.
com: The philosopher Gilbert Ryle, in 1949, distinguished "knowing that" from "knowing how". The terms declarative, used more in psychology, and explicit, used more in knowledge management, are close and often treated as synonyms. It is the kind of knowledge a book or this guide conveys: data, definitions, arguments. It is necessary, but not enough to hold a good conversation; that also takes procedural knowledge. See Procedural knowledge, Tacit knowledge and Surface learning.

def: Knowledge of how to do something, acquired and refined through practice; "knowing how", such as cooking, riding a bike or handling a difficult conversation.
com: Knowing all the arguments doesn't guarantee knowing how to use them: listening carefully, noticing what the person really means, staying calm and choosing the right answer at the right moment are skills learned through practice. That's why the guide has the simulated debate and the flashcard practice, which train responding, not just reading. See Declarative (or explicit) knowledge, Tacit knowledge and Deep learning.

def: Knowledge gained through experience and observation, which can be tested against evidence; in Brazilian schooling, also everyday practical knowledge without systematic method, as opposed to scientific knowledge.
com: In philosophy, it is contrasted with a priori knowledge, which doesn't depend on experience, like that of logic and mathematics. Many questions in the debate about animals are empirical: whether an animal feels pain, how much a diet pollutes, whether a vegan diet is adequate. They are settled by observation and research. Others are moral: whether an animal's suffering counts, and how much. Separating the two kinds of question avoids confusion, because no data alone decides what we should do, and no principle alone decides the facts. See Evidence, Epistemology and Tacit knowledge.

def: Knowledge we have and use but can't fully explain in words, such as recognizing a face or sensing that an animal isn't well.
com: The concept comes from the philosopher and chemist Michael Polanyi, in *The Tacit Dimension* (1966), summed up in the phrase "we can know more than we can tell". It is learned by living and practising alongside those who already know. Sanctuary caretakers, for example, often notice that an animal is ill from their posture or the way they move before any test. This knowledge is valuable, but it is worth confirming with systematic observation, because intuition can also be wrong. See Procedural knowledge, Declarative (or explicit) knowledge and Empirical knowledge.

def: In Brazil, people who rescue, treat, neuter and rehome abandoned or at-risk animals, above all dogs and cats, often on their own; called independent rescuers when they work without an organization.
com: The Portuguese term, literally "animal protectors", can be confusing, because "protecting animals" could include all of them, but in Brazilian usage it usually refers to companion and street animals. The tradition goes back a long way: the União Internacional Protetora dos Animais (UIPA) was founded in São Paulo in 1895. Today much of the work is done by individuals, mostly women, who take animals into their homes, pay for vet care and food out of their own pockets and organize adoption fairs, at a high financial and emotional cost. The closest English terms are animal rescuer or independent rescuer, and someone who takes animals in temporarily is a foster carer; "animal protection" in English usually covers all animals, including those raised for food. Being a rescuer doesn't imply being vegan, and many rescuers eat meat; the reverse also holds, because veganism doesn't replace caring for the animals who already need help. Both kinds of work start from the same concern, and each can learn from the other. See Rescue, Adoption, Fostering (temporary adoption), Foster carer, Castration, Pet and Activism.

def: Taking a rescued animal into a home temporarily, until they recover and find a permanent home; in Brazil, also called "lar temporário" (temporary home).
com: It is one of the foundations of the work of rescuers and organizations, which rarely have room for all the animals they rescue. In the home, the animal recovers from illness or surgery, loses their fear of people and learns to live with others, which improves their chances of adoption, and a place opens up for another rescue. Usually the organization or rescuer in charge handles neutering, vaccines and the search for an adopter, and agrees with the family on who pays for food and vet care. See Foster carer, Adoption, Rescue and Animal rescuers (Brazil's "protetores de animais").

def: A person or family who takes a rescued animal into their home for a period, until the animal is permanently adopted; in Portuguese, "adotante temporário".
com: The role takes time and patience, often dealing with sick, fearful or traumatized animals, plus saying goodbye when the animal goes to a permanent home. Sometimes the bond grows too strong and the family ends up adopting the animal, which is humorously called a "foster fail". For those who can't adopt for good, fostering is a concrete way to help, because each temporary home makes one more rescue possible. See Fostering (temporary adoption), Animal rescuers (Brazil's "protetores de animais") and Adoption.

def: A position at the far end of a spectrum; in political use, ideologies or actions that reject democratic rules, pluralism and the rights of others, often accepting intimidation or violence.
com: What counts as extreme depends on what a society considers normal, and that reference point shifts over time. In a society shaped by moral anthropocentrism, speciesism and carnism, someone who simply stops eating and using animals is called an extremist, while breeding and killing more than 80 billion land animals a year, most of them confined, seems moderate only because it is common. The label describes distance from custom, not the seriousness of what is advocated: refusing to take part in a harm is a more restrained position than inflicting it. Martin Luther King, in his *Letter from Birmingham Jail* (1963), answered the label by saying the question was not whether to be an extremist, but for what cause. Two cautions: there have indeed been violent actions in the name of animals, which this guide rejects, but they don't represent the vast majority of vegans; and turning the label around, calling meat eaters extremists, also shuts the conversation down. See Radicalism, Carnism, Moral anthropocentrism and Speciesism.

def: An epidemic that spreads across several countries or continents and affects a large number of people, such as the 1918 flu, the HIV pandemic and COVID-19.
com: Most recent pandemics began with viruses from animals. According to the UN biodiversity panel (IPBES), in 2020, the main risk factors for new pandemics are land-use change, the expansion and intensification of agriculture and livestock farming, and the trade and consumption of wild animals. Animal farming plays a real part in this, as shown by the 2009 flu pandemic, which originated in pigs. But most zoonoses come from wild animals, and the origin of COVID-19 is still debated. That's why the guide recommends not saying that "going vegan prevents pandemics", but that eating fewer animals reduces one of the risk factors. See One Health, Zoonosis, Antimicrobial resistance and Industrial livestock farming.

def: A bacterium resistant to several antibiotics, sometimes to almost all those available, which makes the infections it causes hard or impossible to treat.
com: The name is popular, not technical: specialists speak of multidrug-resistant bacteria. They emerge and spread through excessive or inappropriate antibiotic use, in human medicine and in animal farming, where drugs are often given to healthy animals. One example is the mcr-1 gene, which confers resistance to colistin, a last-resort antibiotic, identified in 2015 in pigs and chickens in China. See Antimicrobial resistance, Zoonosis and Industrial livestock farming.

def: An approach that treats human health, animal health and environmental health as interconnected, and proposes that they be cared for together across different fields and governments.
com: It is adopted jointly by the World Health Organization, the FAO, the World Organisation for Animal Health and the UN Environment Programme, which since 2022 have worked as a four-organization alliance on the subject. Its main focuses are preventing zoonoses and pandemics, antimicrobial resistance and food safety. In the debate about animals, it gives scientific grounding to a true point: reducing intensive farming, antibiotic use in healthy animals, the wildlife trade and deforestation is a public health prevention measure. It's worth noting that, in One Health, animal health is usually treated mainly as a means to protect humans, not for the sake of the animals themselves. See Zoonosis, Pandemic, Antimicrobial resistance and Superbug.

def: Pleasure in causing others to suffer or in watching them suffer; the term comes from the name of the French writer the Marquis de Sade and was popularized by the psychiatrist Richard von Krafft-Ebing in 1886.
com: Psychology studies everyday sadism as a personality trait, present to different degrees in people: in a 2013 study, Erin Buckels, Daniel Jones and Delroy Paulhus found that some participants chose, and even enjoyed, grinding up insects in a machine that in fact didn't harm them. Animal cruelty is also tracked by authorities as a warning sign of violence against people; since 2016, the FBI has recorded these crimes separately. But most of the suffering imposed on animals doesn't come from sadism, but from indifference, habit and profit: people who eat meat almost never take pleasure in the animal's suffering, and would rather not think about it. That's why calling meat eaters sadists is as inaccurate as calling them psychopaths. There are exceptions where suffering is part of the spectacle, such as bullfights and animal fights, and there the word may fit better. See Animal cruelty, Bullfighting and Rodeo.

def: In debate, using people who live in very different situations as a shield to justify one's own choices, such as Indigenous peoples, the species' ancestors or people in extreme poverty.
com: It shows up in lines like "what about Indigenous people who hunt?", "our ancestors ate meat" or "what about people who go hungry?", said by someone who lives in none of those situations. The other person's circumstances, which may involve a lack of alternatives, survival or a culture of their own, are used to justify a choice made in very different conditions, such as buying meat at the supermarket. This has two problems: it changes the subject, because the question was about the person deciding, and it uses those people as a tool for the argument, without really considering their lives. The guide answers these cases on their own terms, in arguments such as "Indigenous and traditional peoples eat animals", "Poor people have no access" and "Eating meat made us evolve". The name comes from "token", a symbol, and recalls tokenism, the merely symbolic inclusion of members of a group; not to be confused with tokenization in computing, the replacement of data with a code. See Instrumentalization and Double standard.

def: Outrage at some cases of harm or injustice and indifference to similar, or even greater, ones that are routine or involve those close to us.
com: With animals, it is very common. The Yulin festival in China, where dogs are killed for food, draws protests worldwide, while billions of pigs and chickens are killed every year without drawing attention. The killing of Cecil the lion by a hunter in Zimbabwe in 2015 moved millions of people who eat animals every day. Outrage tends to follow the beloved species, the rarity of the case or cultural distance, not the size of the harm. That is why it is so often aimed at the practices of other peoples or of minorities, such as religious sacrifice, while the majority's practices are left out. Outrage itself isn't the problem, since it shows the person cares; the problem is the selectivity, which reveals a double standard. The same yardstick applies to animal advocates: being outraged only at what others do, and not at one's own choices, repeats the mistake. See Double standard, Speciesism and Instrumentalization.

def: An expression used by the legal scholar Gary Francione, in *Introduction to Animal Rights* (2000), to describe the contradiction of saying that animals matter while treating them as things: loving the dog and eating the pig, condemning cruelty and paying for it.
com: The contradiction the term points to is real, and psychology studies it under other names, such as the meat paradox and cognitive dissonance. The name, however, is criticized, and rightly so. Schizophrenia is a serious mental disorder, involving symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations, not a "split personality" nor mere inconsistency. Using the word as a metaphor for contradiction reinforces a mistaken idea of the illness and associates people who live with it with something negative, which feeds the stigma they already face. That's why mental health organizations advise against using diagnoses as metaphors. For a cause that criticizes discrimination, it's worth choosing words that don't demean another group: moral inconsistency, moral dissonance or the meat paradox describe the same problem without that cost. See Cognitive dissonance, Moral consistency and Speciesist term.

def: A person who became vegetarian and stays that way for a long time, even while recognizing the reasons for veganism and knowing that consuming milk, eggs and other animal products still causes suffering and death.
com: The expression is informal and critical, but it need not be an insult: it points to a stop halfway along the road. Someone who stops eating meat for the animals already recognizes that they matter, and milk and egg production also involves exploitation and death, such as the calves separated from their mothers and the male chicks culled at hatching. What usually sustains the stop is the feeling of already doing something important, a case of moral licensing: one step taken becomes a reason not to take the next. Fair criticism doesn't treat the vegetarian as an enemy, since they already reduce harm, but it recalls that the same reason that led to the first change calls for the next. See Vegetarian, Vegan and Perpetual vegan.

def: A vegan who, after learning about the speciesist attitudes they still hold and the broader questions of animal ethics, rejects those questions or takes a very long time to change, as if veganism were the finish line.
com: It is the same idea as the perpetual vegetarian, applied one step further. Veganism rejects animal exploitation, but the reason behind it, taking seriously the interests of those who feel, goes beyond exploitation: it calls for attention to all sentient beings, including fish and invertebrates, to wild animals suffering from natural causes and to minds that may arise in the future. For coherence, someone who is vegan for the animals needs to strive to be antispeciesist, and the road doesn't end at veganism. As with the vegetarian, the criticism is not meant to belittle someone who has already changed a lot, but to recall that the same principle still applies. See Speciesist vegan, Antispeciesism, Sentientism and Perpetual vegetarian.

def: A current in political philosophy holding that justice and moral values arise from the traditions, practices and shared understandings of each community, rather than from universal, abstract principles.
com: It gained ground in the 1980s as a critique of John Rawls's liberalism, with Alasdair MacIntyre (*After Virtue*, 1981), Michael Sandel (*Liberalism and the Limits of Justice*, 1982), Michael Walzer (*Spheres of Justice*, 1983) and Charles Taylor. For animals, it cuts both ways: a state that promotes common values can ban cruel practices that liberalism would leave to individual choice, but if the standard is whatever the community already values, vaquejada, bullfighting and factory farming get the seal of tradition. Mary Midgley and J. Baird Callicott tried to include animals through ties of community, which also makes room for putting those close to us first. Critics such as Alasdair Cochrane, in *An Introduction to Animals and Political Theory* (2010), reply that custom does not justify harm and that protecting animals requires a standard that doesn't depend on majority approval. See Contextual universalism and particularism, Mixed community, Cultural relativism and Liberalism.

def: The policy of recognising a country's cultural and religious diversity, which sometimes includes exempting certain communities from general rules, such as animal protection laws.
com: Examples include religious slaughter without prior stunning, allowed for Jews and Muslims in countries such as the United Kingdom, and, in Brazil, the 2019 Supreme Federal Court ruling in RE 494601, which upheld a Rio Grande do Sul law allowing animal sacrifice in Afro-Brazilian religious rites. Advocates such as Will Kymlicka (*Multicultural Citizenship*, 1995) and Bhikhu Parekh see these exemptions as a way of treating minorities with equal respect. Paula Casal, in the article "Is Multiculturalism Bad for Animals?" (2003), argues that an exemption protects the practice, not the animals, and that the inconsistency of tolerating the cruelty of factory farming is a reason to fight both, not to create new exceptions. There is also the opposite risk: law and outrage tend to target minority practices and spare those of the majority, which is a double standard and can feed racism, as Claire Jean Kim (*Dangerous Crossings*, 2015), Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka discuss. A consistent yardstick applies the same criterion to the religious shrine, the slaughterhouse and the rodeo. See Selective outrage, Cultural relativism, Double standard and Vaquejada.

def: The principle that the state should stay neutral among citizens' different conceptions of the good life, limiting itself to securing rights and freedoms, summed up as the priority of the right over the good.
com: It is a central idea of John Rawls, above all in *Political Liberalism* (1993), and of Ronald Dworkin. The risk for animals is that how we treat them gets classed as a matter of taste or private belief, like religion or lifestyle, on which the state should take no side; veganism then becomes just one worldview among others. Rawls himself granted that cruelty to animals is wrong, but placed it outside justice. Authors such as Robert Garner, Alasdair Cochrane, Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka reply that neutrality applies to choices that affect oneself, not to harm done to others: if animals' interests count, protecting them is a matter of justice, like banning violence against humans, not the imposition of an ideal of life. See Liberalism, Personal choice, Liberal veganism and Original position and veil of ignorance.

pt: Posição original e véu da ignorância
termo: Original position and veil of ignorance
def: John Rawls's thought experiment in which people choose principles of justice without knowing what place they would occupy in society, such as their class, race, sex or talents.
com: It was set out in *A Theory of Justice* (1971): behind the veil, no one can shape the rules in their own favour, so the rules chosen would be fair. Rawls left species out: those choosing know they are human and have a sense of justice, and animals fall outside the scope of justice. Donald VanDeVeer, in 1979, and Mark Rowlands, in a 1997 article and in the book *Animals Like Us* (2002), proposed hiding species, or rationality, behind the veil too: someone who might be born a pig on a factory farm would hardly approve of that system. Robert Garner objects that the outcome depends on the convictions about fairness built into the starting point, and Rawls himself acknowledged that our relations with animals lie outside what his theory sets out to cover. See Contractualism, Impartiality, Reflective equilibrium and Moral person (Rawls).

def: A method of justifying moral principles by adjusting them, back and forth, to our considered judgements about particular cases until principles and judgements form a coherent whole.
com: The name comes from John Rawls in *A Theory of Justice* (1971), who drew in part on how Nelson Goodman justified the rules of induction (*Fact, Fiction, and Forecast*, 1955); Norman Daniels later developed the wide version, which also brings in background theories. For animal ethics, the sensitive point is that considered judgements can carry prejudice: if it seems intuitive that only humans count, the method tends to confirm speciesism. Peter Singer, in 1974, criticised the weight given to intuitions, noting that many of them are leftovers of custom and self-interest. Robert Garner observed that in Rawls the exclusion of animals comes from these starting convictions, not from the contract. Defenders of the method reply that it also allows intuitions to be revised when they clash with well-grounded principles, and the argument from marginal cases works exactly that way. See Original position and veil of ignorance, Argument from marginal cases, Moral universality and Moral consistency.

def: A theory of justice that assesses well-being by what each being is able to do and to be, that is, by its real opportunities to exercise the functions proper to its form of life.
com: It was created by the economist Amartya Sen, starting with the lecture "Equality of What?" (1979), and extended to animals by the philosopher Martha Nussbaum in *Frontiers of Justice* (2006) and *Justice for Animals* (2023). It goes beyond pain: a circus bear that doesn't suffer, but lives caged, dressed up and performing tricks, is still deprived of foraging, exploring and living socially as a bear, and that is already a harm. It thus protects more than an accounting of pleasure and pain alone and fits with the idea of telos. Critics point to three problems: defining what flourishing means for each species can be used to justify whatever is natural, predation included; moving sentience out of the centre would open the door to plants and ecosystems, which Nussbaum avoids by requiring sentience; and lists of capabilities help little in settling conflicts of interest. See Telos, Animal welfare, Sentience and Utilitarianism.

pt: Direitos baseados em interesses (teoria do interesse)
def: The theory that to have a right is to have an interest strong enough to impose duties on others, without depending on the ability to make choices or enter agreements.
com: It stands opposed to the will (or choice) theory, associated with H. L. A. Hart, for which only those who can exercise or waive a right can hold it. Joel Feinberg, in "The Rights of Animals and Unborn Generations" (1974), argued that having interests is the condition for having rights, and Joseph Raz gave the best-known formulation in *The Morality of Freedom* (1986). Since sentient animals have interests, the theory grants them rights without requiring reason or reciprocity, and the same holds for babies and people with severe cognitive disabilities. Alasdair Cochrane uses it to argue that animals have a right not to suffer, but not always a right to liberty, a position abolitionists criticise for leaving room for using animals without suffering. Another open question is how to weigh conflicting interests, since not every interest generates a right. See Interest, Rights, Animal rights and Subjects-of-a-life.

def: The capacity to have preferences and to act to satisfy them, without needing to reflect on moral principles; a criterion proposed by Tom Regan as an alternative to Kantian autonomy.
com: In *The Case for Animal Rights* (1983), Regan distinguished Kantian autonomy, which requires acting on rules one could will to be universal and which only adult humans would have, from preference autonomy, which many animals have: a dog choosing where to lie down or a pig searching for food acts on its own behalf. It is one of the traits that make someone a subject-of-a-life and, for Regan, grounds a right to respectful treatment, that is, never to be used merely as a means. Steven Wise and Evelyn Pluhar followed the same line in extending basic rights to animals on the basis of their capacity to act. The sentientist objection is that the criterion still leaves out sentient animals with simpler mental lives; the opposite objection, from Kantians and contractualists, is that preference is not autonomy in the moral sense. See Autonomy, Subjects-of-a-life, Moral agent and Moral patient.

def: The philosopher Mary Midgley's term for the community formed by humans and animals who live together and form bonds, above all domesticated ones, to whom we would have duties based on closeness.
com: Midgley introduced it in *Animals and Why They Matter* (1983) to show that human societies have always included animals and that partiality towards those close to us can extend to them too. J. Baird Callicott took up the idea in 1988, separating duties to domesticated animals, in the mixed community, from duties to wild ones, in the biotic community, where only the integrity of the ecosystem would count, which would permit culling wild animals to control populations. Proposals such as Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka's in *Zoopolis* (2011), which argue for citizenship for domesticated animals, follow the same intuition. The antispeciesist critique is twofold: if closeness justifies putting humans first, it would also justify putting whites or men first; and a wild animal's suffering weighs no less because the animal is far from us. See Partiality, Communitarianism, Domestic animal and Wild animal suffering.

def: Two positions on where standards of justice come from: particularism says they come from each community's shared understandings; contextual universalism accepts universal values but says each culture interprets and realises them in its own way.
com: Particularism is associated with Michael Walzer, in *Spheres of Justice* (1983), and contextual universalism with Bhikhu Parekh, in *Rethinking Multiculturalism* (2000). Particularism has a serious problem: if justice is whatever each community accepts, no locally accepted cruel practice could be criticised, whether against humans or animals. Contextual universalism seems more reasonable, but it has a limit: not every practice can pass as a local interpretation of a principle, and calling vaquejada or bullfighting a cultural form of respecting animals empties the principle. The useful distinction is between the way a value is applied, which can vary, and the exception that cancels it, which cannot. See Cultural relativism, Moral relativism, Moral universality and Communitarianism.

def: Historical materialism is Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels's thesis that the way a society produces its material life shapes its institutions and ideas; species-being is, for Marx, the human essence expressed in free, conscious labour.
com: The concept of species-being appears in the *Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts* of 1844, and historical materialism was set out in *The German Ideology* (1845-1846). Marx defined the human by contrast with the animal: the animal would produce only for immediate need, the human freely and universally; the alienated worker would be reduced to the animal functions of eating, drinking and procreating. Ted Benton, in *Natural Relations* (1993), criticised this dualism and showed that many human needs are shared with other animals, bringing Marxism closer to animal ethics; authors such as David Nibert link animal exploitation to capitalism. At the same time, historical materialism helps explain how factory farming, the turning of animals into commodities and the hiding of slaughter arise from economic interests, not from a fixed human nature. See Alienation, Socialism, Commodification and Animal exploitation.

def: A principle of distributive justice summed up in the formula "from each according to their abilities, to each according to their needs".
com: The formula circulated among French socialists such as Louis Blanc and became famous through Karl Marx in the *Critique of the Gotha Programme* (1875), as the motto of an advanced phase of communism. Since animals also have needs, authors such as David Sztybel and Ted Benton have argued that limiting the principle to humans is speciesism, and Benton argues that people find it easier to recognise needs in animals than rights. There are objections: Marx had a society of abundance in mind, not conflicts under scarcity; not every need weighs the same; and without a criterion such as sentience, the idea of need would also cover plants and microorganisms. Even so, the formula leaves a direct lesson: an animal's basic need should outweigh a trivial human preference, such as taste. See Necessity, Socialism, Historical materialism and species-being and Interest.

def: The idea that only those who can give something in return, cooperate or keep agreements with others are owed justice or certain rights.
com: It underlies contractualism, from Thomas Hobbes to David Gauthier (*Morals by Agreement*, 1986), and appears in John Rawls, for whom society is a system of cooperation for mutual advantage. Peter Carruthers, in *The Animals Issue* (1992), used it to deny that we have direct duties to animals. The problem is that the criterion also excludes babies, people with severe cognitive disabilities and future generations, who cannot reciprocate; those who try to include them usually fall back on another criterion, which shows that reciprocity was not the real criterion. It also confuses who can be party to an agreement with who can be harmed by it: animals don't negotiate, but they bear the consequences. See Contractualism, Argument from marginal cases, Moral agent and Moral patient.

def: For John Rawls, a being with the capacity to form a conception of their own good and a sense of justice, a sufficient condition for being owed justice.
com: Rawls defined the term in *A Theory of Justice* (1971), in the section on the basis of equality, and concluded that animals, not being moral persons, fall outside justice, although cruelty to them is wrong. He treated this capacity as a sufficient condition, without saying whether it was necessary, and included children because they have the capacity potentially, but left vague the position of humans who will never have it. This is where the argument from marginal cases comes in: if justice applies to all humans, including those who lack these capacities, the real boundary is species, not moral personality. The notion is close to that of moral agent, but the question is different: Rawls is not asking who can be held responsible, but to whom justice is owed. See Moral agent, Moral patient, Original position and veil of ignorance and Argument from marginal cases.

def: Ronald Dworkin's principle that the state must treat each person with equal concern, for their interests and well-being, and equal respect, for their life choices.
com: Dworkin set it out in *Taking Rights Seriously* (1977), while interpreting John Rawls's theory, and developed it in *Sovereign Virtue* (2000). He restricted it to humans able to make plans and act justly, but the two halves have different sources: respect is tied to autonomy, while concern comes from our being beings who feel and have needs, which is also true of sentient animals. For this reason, authors such as Alasdair Cochrane argue that the concern half extends naturally to animals, even if the respect half applies to them differently. Not to be confused with Peter Singer's equal consideration of interests: Dworkin's is a principle about how the state treats its members; Singer's is a general moral principle about the weight of similar interests. See Equal consideration, Autonomy, Liberalism and Justice.

def: Harms that sentient beings suffer from causes that do not come from human practices, such as disease, parasites, hunger, cold, predation and disasters.
com: Luciano Carlos Cunha uses the expression in *Razões para ajudar* (2022, in Portuguese) as a synonym for non-anthropogenic harms and acknowledges that the label is debatable, because it seems to place humans outside nature. For anyone who looks at the suffering animal, the origin of the harm does not change what they feel: a fracture caused by a fall hurts as much as one caused by a trap, and for this reason Cunha and Oscar Horta deny that natural harms are value-neutral. A frequent confusion, pointed out by Horta, is to call anthropocentric what is merely anthropogenic: help decided on and carried out by humans is anthropogenic, but it would only be anthropocentric if it aimed at the good of humans and ignored that of the animals. Those who defend letting nature take its course usually accept the duty not to cause harm and reject the duty to prevent natural harms, and this asymmetry is at the heart of the debate about wild animals. See Suffering from natural causes, Wild animal suffering, Anthropocentrism and Equivalence thesis.

def: The branch of ecology that studies how the size of populations changes over time, according to rates of birth, death and migration.
com: One of its most important data points for ethics is age-specific mortality, that is, the proportion of animals of a species that die at each stage of life, summarized in life tables and survivorship curves. In most species, which lay hundreds or thousands of eggs, almost all offspring die shortly after birth, a pattern ecologists call a type III survivorship curve. Authors such as Oscar Horta, Catia Faria and Luciano Carlos Cunha use these data to argue that, if these young animals can already feel, an early death, often from hunger or predation, is the typical experience of a wild animal. The most debated empirical point is when sentience begins in these early stages, which is still uncertain in many groups, such as fish and insect larvae. See Carrying capacity, r and K reproductive strategies, Altricial and precocial animals and Wild animal suffering.

def: The maximum population size of a species that an environment can sustain over time, given the available resources, represented in models by the letter K.
com: The concept appears in the logistic equation, proposed by the Belgian mathematician Pierre-François Verhulst in 1838, in which a population's growth slows as it approaches K. In wild animal ethics, the central point is that the number of offspring born is usually far greater than the carrying capacity, so that in a stable population the surplus dies, generally early. For this reason, providing more food without controlling births may only increase the number of animals that are born and die, which is why proposals such as contraception come up in this debate. Ecologists criticize the use of carrying capacity as a fixed number, since it varies with climate, with other species and over time. See Population dynamics, r and K reproductive strategies and Animal population control.

def: The distinction between species that have many offspring and invest little in each (r-strategists) and species that have few offspring and care for them (K-strategists).
com: The letters come from the logistic equation: r is the population's growth rate and K the carrying capacity. The theory of r/K selection was formulated by Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson in 1967 and extended by Eric Pianka in 1970, who attached to it a series of predictions about other traits of animals. Today it is considered outdated in ecology and has given way to life-history theory, which speaks of a continuum between fast and slow life histories, as David Reznick and colleagues show in a 2002 review; the basic distinction between having many or few offspring, however, remains valid, as Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) notes. "Strategy" is a metaphor, because animals do not plan how they reproduce. The ethical point is that most animals are born into species of the first kind, in which almost all offspring die soon, although Heather Browning and Walter Veit (2023) dispute that this implies as much suffering as is usually assumed. See Population dynamics, Carrying capacity and Wild animal suffering.

def: A classification of animals by their degree of development at birth or hatching: precocial animals are born relatively mature and mobile, while altricial animals are born underdeveloped and depend on parental care.
com: Classic examples are foals and ducklings, which are precocial, and songbird chicks and human babies, which are altricial; Augustine, Lika and Kooijman (2019) show that this is a continuum, not two boxes. The distinction matters in the debate about wild animal suffering because it is sometimes said that young animals who die early do not yet feel anything. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that being immature is not the same as not being sentient, and that most small animals with many offspring are precocial, that is, they must fend for themselves from very early on. The empirical question, however, remains open: for many larvae and fish fry it is not known when sentience begins. See Sentience, Population dynamics and r and K reproductive strategies.

def: The idea that nature, left to itself, tends towards a stable and harmonious state in which populations remain constant.
com: The notion comes from the ancient idea of the "balance of nature" and is still widely used to reject any help for wild animals. In ecology, however, it has no single definition: the ecologist Charles Elton was already writing in 1930 that this balance does not exist, and Volker Grimm and Christian Wissel (1997) gathered more than 160 definitions of stability, to the point of considering the term nearly useless. Ecosystems are now seen as dynamic, open and subject to disturbance. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) adds that, even where there is something like stability, it is maintained precisely because most offspring die, so that balance does not mean the well-being of individuals. This does not make ecological risk irrelevant: poorly planned interventions can make things worse, which is why those who defend helping wild animals call for research before action. See Idyllic nature, Ecology, Holism and Wild animal suffering.

def: In environmental ethics, the view that gives direct moral consideration to non-sentient wholes, such as species, ecosystems or the biotic community.
com: Its landmark is Aldo Leopold's land ethic, in *A Sand County Almanac* (1949), developed by J. Baird Callicott and Holmes Rolston III; ecocentrism is the variant in which the valuable whole is the ecosystem. Since value lies in the whole, a consistent holist may accept killing individuals to protect a species or an ecosystem, a consequence Tom Regan, in *The Case for Animal Rights* (1983), called "environmental fascism". From a sentientist point of view, species and ecosystems feel nothing and matter only through their effect on those who feel; hence the conflict with helping wild animals, which holism tends to reject when it alters natural processes. Holists answer that the individual-centred approach ignores ecological interdependence and may have disastrous consequences. See Holistic environmentalism, Ecocentrism, Naturocentrism and Biocentrism.

def: The view that gives direct moral value to what is natural because of its origin, that is, because it was not produced or altered by humans.
com: Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) uses the term to distinguish this position from holism: for naturocentrism, it is not enough for something to have certain characteristics; it must have arisen from natural processes. An example is Robert Elliot's article "Faking Nature" (1982), according to which an area restored by humans is worth less than the original, even if identical, just as a forgery is worth less than the authentic work; Eric Katz defended a similar idea in 1992. The sentientist criticism is that the origin of a harm does not change what it does to the one who suffers it: hunger caused by a drought hurts no less than hunger caused by humans. Critics also point out that the position assumes humans stand outside nature, a separation many philosophers and ecologists reject. See Holism, Natural harms, Naturalistic fallacy and Biocentrism.

def: In ecology, the study of how predation risk changes the behaviour, physiology and distribution of prey, even when they are not killed.
com: The concept was proposed by Joel Brown, John Laundré and Mahesh Gurung in a 1999 article, and from it comes the idea of the "landscape of fear", the map of places prey avoid out of fear of predators. In conservation, the expression has also come to mean the reintroduction of predators, such as wolves in Yellowstone National Park, in the United States, from 1995, so that fear drives deer and other herbivores away from plants one wants to protect. The cascading effect attributed to the Yellowstone wolves is debated among ecologists, who disagree about how much of the vegetation's recovery is due to them. Oscar Horta (2010) and Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) criticize the practice: it uses the fear, hunger and death of sentient animals as tools for environmental goals, and shows that intervening in nature is already accepted when the aim is not the good of the animals. See Predation, Holism, Conservation biology and Wild animal suffering.

def: The applied science that studies how to protect biological diversity, that is, species, populations and ecosystems, from threats of extinction and degradation.
com: The field was defined by Michael Soulé in the article "What Is Conservation Biology?" (1985), which also gave it value postulates, such as the claim that biological diversity has value in itself. In it, animals are studied mainly as members of species or parts of ecosystems, and the suffering of each one usually takes second place, which explains why killing animals of invasive species is common practice. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) distinguishes it from welfare biology, which studies what is good or bad for animals as sentient individuals, and from two intermediate fields, compassionate conservation and conservation welfare. These areas use similar knowledge, such as ecology and population dynamics, but have different ultimate goals. See Welfare biology, Compassionate conservation, Conservation welfare and Invasive alien species.

def: A current in conservation that defends protecting species and ecosystems without causing unnecessary harm to individual animals.
com: A landmark of the movement is the collection *Ignoring Nature No More* (2013), edited by the ethologist Marc Bekoff, and its principles are usually summed up as "first, do no harm", "individuals matter", inclusivity and peaceful coexistence. Arian Wallach and colleagues (2018) defended the approach in the journal *Conservation Biology*, and Matt Hayward and colleagues (2019) replied in the same journal that it picks mammal examples, ignores the native animals killed by invasive predators and may weaken conservation. From a sentientist point of view, compassionate conservation is an advance, but a limited one: as Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) notes, it deals mainly with the harms caused by conservation actions themselves, not with the natural harms that most wild animals suffer. That is why he distinguishes it from welfare biology. See Conservation biology, Conservation welfare, Welfare biology and Invasive alien species.

def: A field that combines conservation biology with animal welfare science to assess and improve the welfare of wild animals affected by conservation actions.
com: The expression was proposed by the New Zealand scientist Ngaio Beausoleil and colleagues in 2018, and in the article "I Am a Compassionate Conservation Welfare Scientist" (2020) she explained why the field is not the same as compassionate conservation: it accepts the goals of conservation and seeks to reduce harms to animals step by step, working with conservationists, rather than starting from principles such as "first, do no harm". The field may also study how natural harms, or harms indirectly caused by humans, affect welfare, when these data serve conservation. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) notes that this knowledge may be useful to welfare biology, but the ultimate goal is different: here welfare matters within the limits of conservation, there it matters for its own sake. Organizations such as Wild Animal Initiative see the field as a bridge between conservationists and those concerned with wild animals. See Conservation biology, Compassionate conservation, Welfare biology and Animal welfare.

def: Any modification of the conditions of the natural environment that has a net positive effect on the well-being of the sentient individuals living there.
com: The definition is by the Portuguese philosopher Catia Faria, in her thesis *Animal Ethics Goes Wild* (2016) and her book *Animal Ethics in the Wild* (Cambridge University Press, 2022). Faria argues that if we have a duty to meet the needs of wild animals, and if preserving natural environments means maintaining the suffering and death of most of them, then we have an obligation, not merely a permission, to change these environments for the better. The proposal reverses the common idea that our duty towards nature is to preserve it as it is. Critics, from environmentalists to some animal advocates such as Clare Palmer, point to the risk of unforeseen effects and to disrespect for the independent lives of wild animals, and Faria herself discusses, in a 2023 article, how to keep interventions from creating new vulnerabilities. See Natural harms, Welfare biology, Wild animal suffering and Idyllic nature.

def: Categories from Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka's political theory: liminal animals are non-domesticated animals who live among humans, such as pigeons and rats, and animal sovereignty is the right of communities of wild animals to govern themselves in their own territory.
com: In *Zoopolis* (2011), the authors propose that our obligations to animals depend on the political relationship: domesticated animals would be citizens, liminal animals denizens with rights of their own, and wild animals sovereign communities, like foreign nations. From this they conclude that we should respect the autonomy of wild animals and intervene only in limited cases, although they accept that intervening is sometimes permissible and even obligatory. Oscar Horta (2013) and Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answer that the analogy with nations does not fit well: animals who are born by the hundreds and almost all die within a few days do not form communities capable of self-government, and the border between human and wild territory does not change what each animal feels. Defenders of the approach reply that it avoids paternalism and takes seriously the lives wild animals lead without us. See Synanthropic animals, Mixed community, Paternalism and Wild animal suffering.

def: Interfering with someone's freedom or choices against their will, with the aim of benefiting them.
com: The name recalls the authority of parents over their children, and the classic philosophical discussion is Gerald Dworkin's article "Paternalism" (1972), which distinguishes justifiable cases, such as stopping a child from driving, from cases that disrespect the autonomy of adults. Tom Regan, in the preface to the 2004 edition of *The Case for Animal Rights*, accused the proposal to help wild animals who are victims of natural harms of being paternalistic. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that, for there to be paternalism, help would have to go against what the animal prefers, and no animal prefers to die of hunger or infection; providing food or vaccinating with baits goes against no one's will. The objection has more force against coercive interventions, such as capturing an animal to sterilize them, but even there paternalism is usually accepted with children and domestic animals when the harm prevented is great. See Autonomy, Consent, Liminal animals and animal sovereignty and Wild animal suffering.

def: Terms proposed by Luciano Carlos Cunha to separate two positions usually called welfarism: the one that considers animal exploitation fair as long as it is regulated (normative) and the one that considers it unjust but defends regulating it as a strategy to end it (strategic).
com: Cunha introduces the distinction in *Razões para ajudar* (2022, in Portuguese) to clear up a confusion: since both positions are called welfarism, many people conclude that any concern for animal welfare is reformist, and that defending help for wild animals would be a form of welfarism. It is not: one can reject all exploitation and still care about the well-being of animals, including those who suffer from natural causes. Strategic regulationism corresponds largely to what Gary Francione called new welfarism, in *Rain Without Thunder* (1996). The debate between abolitionists and reformists over whether reforms bring the end of exploitation closer or postpone it remains open. See Welfarism, Neo-welfarism, Abolitionism and Incremental reforms.

def: Describes a morally good and praiseworthy act that goes beyond duty, so that not doing it is not wrong.
com: The modern discussion begins with J. O. Urmson's article "Saints and Heroes" (1958), which drew attention to heroic acts that no one is obliged to perform. The notion only fits some non-consequentialist theories: for consequentialism, there is always a duty to choose the best possible outcome, however difficult. In the debate about wild animals, it is common to accept that helping them is admirable but optional; Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that, even granting the category, the natural harms at stake are so great that helping when the cost is low could hardly be merely praiseworthy. Defenders of the supererogatory argue that a morality with no room for personal choices would be too demanding. See Demandingness objection, Positive and negative duties, Consequentialism and Deontology.

def: A distinction of Kantian origin between duties that hold always and towards everyone, without exception (perfect), and duties that leave room for choice about when, how and towards whom to fulfil them (imperfect).
com: Immanuel Kant used it in the *Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals* (1785) and *The Metaphysics of Morals* (1797): not lying would be a perfect duty, and helping those in need an imperfect one. Negative duties, not to cause harm, are usually associated with perfect duties, and positive duties, to help, with imperfect and weaker ones. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) disputes this association: since agriculture, transport and nearly everything we do kill animals, no one can fulfil negative duties towards all sentient beings, and they only seem perfect in a context that leaves animals out. For him, given the world as it is, both kinds of duty are imperfect, and being imperfect does not necessarily make a duty weaker; this is an original thesis, still little discussed in the literature. See Positive and negative duties, Duties, Deontology and Omission.

def: Negative duties are duties not to do something, such as not to cause harm, and positive duties are duties to do something, such as to help those in need.
com: Many theories, especially deontological and libertarian ones, give negative duties more force than positive ones, and some deny that positive duties exist. On this basis, some animal rights advocates, such as Tom Regan and Gary Francione, argue that we should simply leave wild animals alone. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) argues that the reason for guaranteeing negative rights, protecting vital interests, also justifies positive duties, since these interests can be threatened by hunger, disease or predation, not only by agents. Defenders of the asymmetry answer that causing harm is worse than failing to prevent it, a position associated with Philippa Foot and Warren Quinn. See Duties, Perfect and imperfect duties, Equivalence thesis and Omission.

def: The thesis that the difference between causing a harm and allowing it to happen has no moral importance in itself.
com: It was defended by James Rachels, in the article "Active and Passive Euthanasia" (1975), and, with qualifications, by Peter Singer, in *Practical Ethics* (1979; 2nd ed., 1993). Singer holds that there is no intrinsic difference between killing and letting die, but he grants differences that usually come with the distinction, such as motivation, the certainty of the outcome and causal responsibility; motivation and certainty, for him, carry moral weight, so failing to help those dying in poverty should not be condemned as killing, but is closer to a death caused by reckless driving. He also separates judging the act from the blame the person deserves. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) applies the thesis to wild animals: if it is true, letting an animal die of a disease we could treat is not, in itself, less serious than causing them the disease. Much of deontology rejects the thesis and defends the distinction between doing and allowing, as Philippa Foot, Warren Quinn and Frances Kamm do. Even those who reject the thesis usually accept some duty to help when the cost is low, which is already enough for part of the reasons to help wild animals. See Omission, Positive and negative duties, Natural harms and Consequentialism.

def: The principle that one can only have a duty to do what it is possible to do.
com: It is traditionally attributed to Immanuel Kant and accepted by most moral theories. In the debate about wild animals, it appears as an objection: since it is impossible to help all the animals in nature, there would be no duty to help them. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that the principle only removes the duty to do the impossible, not the duty to do what is within reach, such as vaccinating, rescuing or researching, and that what is impossible today may cease to be so with more knowledge. The principle itself is debated: a study by Vladimir Chituc and colleagues (2016) found that people often judge that someone ought to do what they cannot, when they are to blame for their own inability.
